paragraphs.text: Budgeting is the most widely used accounting tool for planning and controlling organisations
A budget is a quantitative expression of a proposed plan for a future time period and an aid to the coordination and implementation of the plan
Budget provides targets and directions – increase income or decrease expenses
It can cover both financial and non-financial aspects
Planning the performance of the organization (whole and subunits)
Providing a set of expectations (to compare with actual results)
Investigating variations from plans (and corrective actions)
Planning again, considering feedback and changed conditions
The master budget coordinates all the financial projections in the organisation’s individual budgets in a single organisation-wide set of budgets
A master budget is a comprehensive expression of management’s operating and financial plans for a future time period (usually one year)
It embraces the impact of both operating decisions and financing decisions
Operating decisions centre on the use of scarce resources
Financing decisions centre on how to obtain the funds to acquire those resources
The term 'master' in 'master budget' refers to it being a comprehensive, organisation-wide set of budgets
Overall financial and operational plan. Sub-budgets tied together
Summarises the financial projections of all the organisation’s individual budgets
Results in a set of related financial statements for a set time period, usually a year
Based on the principles of activity based costing (ABC) where cost drivers for activities are identified and then costed
Cash planning and Control. Aims to avoid idle cash and possible cash shortage
Part of the master budget that comprises capital budget, cash budget, budgeted balance sheet and budgeted statement of cash flows
Budgeting for long-term projects to be undertaken and capital to be acquired
Appropriate for departments whose work load does not have a direct current relationship to sales
A static budget is a budget that is based on one level of output
It is based on the level of output planned at the start of the budget period
It is not adjusted or altered after it is set
It is prepared at the start of the period when the actual output is known
Performance evaluation is difficult when actual activities differ from the planned level of activity
The master budget is an example of a static budget
A flexible budget shows revenues and expenses that should have occurred at the actual level of activity
A flexible budget is adjusted in accordance with changes in actual output
A flexible budget is prepared at the end of the period when the actual output is known
Flexible budget is used for both better planning and control
A key difference between a flexible budget and a static budget is the use of the actual output level in the flexible budget
Operational budget deals with cost for merchandise and services produced. Financial budget examines expected asset liability and equity
Part of the master budget that comprises the budgeted profit statement
A budget or plan that is always available for a specified future period by adding a month, quarter or year in the future as the month, quarter or year just ended is dropped
A 12-month rolling budget for Mar2018 to Feb2019 becomes a 12-month rolling budget for Apr2018 to Mar2018 and so on
Rolling budgets constantly force management to think concretely about the forthcoming 12 months
Budgets typically have a set time period (month, quarter, year)

Internal Rate of Return vs. Return on Investment
IRR is complex and considers cash flows, time value of money (TVM) and risk

ROI is simple but not comparable, ignores TVM and disregards risk
Financial ratio measuring the profitability of an investment, as a percentage of the invested amount
Avoid: When TVM, cash flows timing, and risk are critical factors in investment decisions

A financial tool used by businesses to evaluate investments, projects, or strategic decisions from the perspective of maximizing shareholder value. The key concept behind the SVA framework is that the primary goal of a business should be to maximize the wealth of its shareholders. To achieve this objective, the framework emphasizes the importance of estimating the net present value (NPV) of future cash flows generated by an investment or decision.

Portfolios constructed to maximize an investor's satisfaction or utility, taking into account their specific risk tolerance and return preferences.
Portfolios designed to minimize exposure to certain risk factors or biases, ensuring they are not overly affected by market movements or specific risks.
Portfolios that balance long and short positions to equalize the dollar value of investments, aiming to neutralize exposure to market direction and focus on relative performance.
Portfolios are structured to have a beta of zero, meaning they aim to eliminate sensitivity to overall market movements, focusing instead on generating returns from stock-specific factors.
The process of converting cash or cash-equivalent holdings into a balanced portfolio of equities to achieve the desired level of market exposure and enhance returns.
A strategy that involves buying (long) stocks expected to increase in value and selling (short) stocks expected to decrease, aiming to profit from the relative performance of the chosen securities.
A strategy that seeks to neutralize market risk by balancing long and short positions so that overall exposure to market movements is minimized, focusing on profiting from stock-specific factors.

A strategy that involves converting a non-equity investment, such as cash or bonds, into a position in equities to gain market exposure and potential returns while managing risks associated with the equity market.

A strategy where investors take a long position in preferred stocks worth 130% of their portfolio’s value and simultaneously short stocks worth 30%, leveraging the portfolio to enhance returns while maintaining a net 100% market exposure.
A strategy that involves buying securities that have shown upward price trends and selling those with downward trends, based on the expectation that these trends will continue for a certain period.
A risk management strategy used to offset potential losses in one investment by taking an opposite position in a related asset, effectively reducing exposure to adverse market movements.
